analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC use antitrust law against nonprofit hospital systems and hospital cooperatives.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would end nonprofit hospitals' exemption from federal antitrust enforcement, died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Federal Trade Commission enforces laws against monopolies and unfair competition, but by long-standing interpretation nonprofit hospitals are generally outside its reach [S3]. This bill would change that: it adds nonprofit hospital organizations and hospital cooperatives to the FTC's antitrust authority [S2] [S3]. The point is to let the FTC challenge hospital mergers and other conduct that consolidates hospital markets and can drive up prices. The bill never moved after being referred to the House Judiciary Committee in April 2023 [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and health care consumers, especially in areas where one hospital system dominates: more FTC scrutiny of hospital mergers could mean more competing providers and less pricing power in a single large system. The FTC itself gains clear authority to act [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Extends the FTC's authority over unfair methods of competition to tax-exempt hospital organizations and cooperative hospital service organizations, which are currently outside that authority [S2] [S3].

Hospitals that are nonprofits are increasingly part of large merged systems; giving the FTC enforcement power is aimed at anticompetitive conduct in health care markets, where consolidation is widely associated with higher prices [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large nonprofit hospital systems, which would lose their practical exemption from FTC antitrust enforcement and could face challenges to mergers and other conduct; costs could be passed to insurers or, in some cases, absorbed as thinner margins [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Hospitals argue many mergers let them share staff, equipment, and costly services, keeping care available in rural areas; aggressive antitrust enforcement could block combinations that supporters see as beneficial [S2].

The bill is a single narrow amendment: it gives the FTC authority but does not itself change hospital pricing, require charity care, or address for-profit hospital consolidation, so its practical effect depends entirely on future enforcement decisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to consumers is real but indirect: the bill only restores the FTC's ability to police nonprofit hospital conduct, and results would depend on future enforcement. The main costs fall on hospital systems that would face new legal scrutiny, and there is a good-faith concern that some combinations that aid rural care could be challenged. On balance it is a targeted, modest consumer-protection measure with limited downside for the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 26, 2023 by Rep. Jayapal with Rep. Spartz and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S3] [S5].
It attracted only three cosponsors (two Democrats and one Republican), and the complete action history shows no further action after the referral to committee [S4] [S5].
The bill expired with the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 without ever leaving committee [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large nonprofit hospital systems came out ahead: they remain outside the FTC's antitrust authority and face no new scrutiny of mergers or market conduct. Health care consumers, who bear the costs of hospital consolidation, gained nothing from the bill's failure to move.

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's Republican co-lead at introduction

for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to expire

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic lead with one Republican co-lead and a 2-1 Democratic-to-Republican cosponsor split — but the tiny total of four members offered no pressure to move the bill.

industries.industry: Nonprofit hospital systems and hospital cooperatives
industries.note: These systems currently sit outside FTC antitrust enforcement; the bill would make their mergers and market conduct subject to federal challenges. Their market power over local pricing and care networks is exactly what the bill targets, and the public bears the cost when consolidation reduces competition.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employers paying hospital rates
industries.note: Payers face hospital systems with consolidated pricing power; FTC enforcement against anticompetitive hospital conduct could ease the negotiating leverage driving premiums and employer health costs.
